html:
The Id Kah Mosque in Kashgar, in Xinjiang, is the largest mosque in China, with room for some 20,000 worshippers in its prayer hall and courtyard. It was built in 1442 on the site of older graves and shrines and enlarged many times since; its yellow brick gate front with two minarets dates mostly from the 1800s.

Kashgar, at the western end of the Tarim Basin where Silk Road routes met before crossing the Pamirs, had been Muslim since the Kara-Khanid rulers converted in the 900s. The square in front of the mosque was the heart of Uyghur city life, where crowds gathered for the Eid festivals that give it its name: Id Kah means "place of the festival".

In recent decades it became a symbol of the struggle over Uyghur identity. Its imam, who backed government policy, was murdered outside it in 2014. Much of Kashgar's old town around it was torn down and rebuilt from 2009, and since about 2016 the mosque has been mostly closed to ordinary worship, part of the wider crackdown that included the internment camps.
